{{Distinguish|modular representation theory|Aschbacher block}}
{{redirect|Block system|the railway signalling system|Signalling block system}}

In [[mathematics]] and [[group theory]], a '''block''' for the [[Group action (mathematics)|action]] of a [[group (mathematics)|group]] <math>G</math> on a [[Set (mathematics)|set]] <math>X</math> is a subset <math>Y</math> of <math>X</math> whose images under <math>G</math> either coincide with <math>Y</math> or are disjoint from <math>Y</math>. These images form a '''block system''', a [[partition (set theory)|partition]] of <math>X</math> that is <math>G</math>-invariant. In terms of the associated [[equivalence relation]] on <math>X</math>, <math>G</math>-invariance means that

{{bi|left=1.6|<math>x\sim y</math> implies <math>gx\sim gy</math>}}

for all <math>g\in G</math> and all <math>x,y\in X</math>. The action of <math>G</math> on <math>X</math> induces a natural action of <math>G</math> on any block system for <math>X</math>.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Seress | first = Ákos
 | doi = 10.1017/CBO9780511546549
 | isbn = 0-521-66103-X
 | mr = 1970241
 | page = [https://books.google.com/books?id=hxFqdbfc_CMC&pg=PA9 9]
 | publisher = Cambridge University Press, Cambridge
 | series = Cambridge Tracts in Mathematics
 | title = Permutation Group Algorithms
 | volume = 152
 | year = 2003}}</ref>

The set of [[orbit (group theory)|orbits]] of the <math>G</math>-set <math>X</math> is an example of a block system. The corresponding equivalence relation is the smallest <math>G</math>-invariant equivalence on <math>X</math> such that the induced action on the block system is trivial.

The partition into [[singleton set]]s is a block system and if <math>X</math> is non-empty then the partition into one set <math>X</math> itself is a block system as well (if <math>X</math> is a singleton set then these two partitions are identical). A [[transitive action|transitive]] (and thus non-empty) <math>G</math>-set <math>X</math> is said to be [[Primitive permutation group|primitive]] if it has no other block systems.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Dixon | first1 = John D.
 | last2 = Mortimer | first2 = Brian
 | doi = 10.1007/978-1-4612-0731-3
 | isbn = 0-387-94599-7
 | mr = 1409812
 | page = [https://books.google.com/books?id=1SPjBwAAQBAJ&pg=PA12 12]
 | publisher = Springer-Verlag, New York
 | series = Graduate Texts in Mathematics
 | title = Permutation Groups
 | volume = 163
 | year = 1996}}</ref> For a non-empty <math>G</math>-set <math>X</math> the transitivity requirement in the previous definition is only necessary in the case when <math>|X|=2</math> and the group action is trivial.

==Stabilizers of blocks==
If ''B'' is a block, the [[stabilizer subgroup|stabilizer]] of ''B'' is the [[subgroup]]
:''G''<sub>''B''</sub> = { ''g'' ∈ ''G'' | ''gB'' = ''B'' }.
The stabilizer of a block contains the stabilizer ''G''<sub>''x''</sub> of each of its elements.  Conversely, if ''x'' ∈ ''X'' and ''H'' is a subgroup of ''G'' containing ''G''<sub>''x''</sub>, then the orbit ''H''.''x'' of ''x'' under ''H'' is a block contained in the orbit ''G''.''x'' and containing ''x''.

For any ''x'' ∈ ''X'', block ''B'' containing ''x'' and subgroup ''H'' ⊆ ''G'' containing ''G''<sub>''x''</sub> it's ''G''<sub>''B''</sub>.''x'' = ''B'' ∩ ''G''.''x'' and ''G''<sub>''H''.''x''</sub> = ''H''.

It follows that the blocks containing ''x'' and contained in ''G''.''x'' are in [[one-to-one correspondence]] with the subgroups of ''G'' containing ''G''<sub>''x''</sub>.  In particular, if the ''G''-set ''X'' is transitive then the blocks containing ''x'' are in one-to-one correspondence with the subgroups of ''G'' containing ''G''<sub>''x''</sub>. In this case the ''G''-set ''X'' is primitive if and only if either the group action is trivial (then ''X'' = {''x''}) or the stabilizer ''G''<sub>''x''</sub> is a [[maximal subgroup]] of ''G'' (then the stabilizers of all elements of ''X'' are the maximal subgroups of ''G'' [[conjugacy class|conjugate]] to ''G''<sub>''x''</sub> because ''G''<sub>''gx''</sub> = ''g'' ⋅ ''G''<sub>''x''</sub> ⋅ ''g''<sup>−''1''</sup>).
